subject: biology
title: Cell structure
summary: Compares prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, follows proteins through the endomembrane system, explains the cytoskeleton and endosymbiosis theory, and practises microscopy and magnification calculations.
body:
Every living thing is made of cells, and every cell comes from an existing cell. How a cell is organised explains why a pancreatic cell can export large amounts of insulin, why some antibiotics kill bacteria without harming us, and why mitochondria carry their own DNA. This lesson compares prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, traces proteins through the endomembrane system, introduces the cytoskeleton and the endosymbiosis theory, and finishes with the microscopy calculations you will use in BIO1011 practicals.

## Key ideas

### Cell theory and why cells are small

**Cell theory** states that all organisms are made of one or more cells, the cell is the basic unit of structure and function, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells. Cells stay small because of the **surface area to volume ratio (SA:V)**. As a cell grows, its volume (which sets how much material it must exchange) rises with the cube of its length, while its surface (where exchange happens) rises only with the square. A cube with 1 µm sides has SA:V = 6 : 1; a cube with 10 µm sides has SA:V = 0.6 : 1. Large cells get around this by being long and thin, folding their membranes (microvilli) or dividing their interior into compartments.

### Prokaryotic cells

**Prokaryotes** (the domains Bacteria and Archaea) have no nucleus. Their DNA is usually a single circular chromosome found in a region called the **nucleoid**, often with small extra DNA circles called **plasmids** that may carry genes such as antibiotic resistance. They have no membrane-bound organelles. Their ribosomes are **70S** (made of 50S and 30S subunits; S is the Svedberg unit, a measure of how fast a particle sediments, so the numbers do not simply add). Most bacteria have a cell wall containing **peptidoglycan**; archaeal walls lack it. Many prokaryotes also have a **capsule**, **pili** for attachment and DNA transfer, and **flagella** that rotate like a propeller. Typical size is 1–5 µm.

### Eukaryotic cells

**Eukaryotes** (animals, plants, fungi and protists) have a **nucleus** surrounded by a **nuclear envelope**, a double membrane with **nuclear pores** that control traffic of RNA and proteins. Their DNA is linear, split into several chromosomes and wrapped around **histone** proteins. Cytosolic ribosomes are **80S** (60S + 40S). Membrane-bound organelles divide the cell into **compartments**, so incompatible reactions (for example, protein digestion in lysosomes and protein synthesis in the cytosol) can run at the same time. Typical size is 10–100 µm.

| Feature | Prokaryotic | Eukaryotic |
|---|---|---|
| Nucleus | Absent (nucleoid) | Present, double membrane |
| DNA | Usually one circular chromosome, plasmids | Several linear chromosomes with histones |
| Ribosomes | 70S | 80S in cytosol (70S in mitochondria and chloroplasts) |
| Membrane-bound organelles | None | Many |
| Cell wall | Peptidoglycan (bacteria) | Cellulose (plants), chitin (fungi), none (animals) |
| Cell division | Binary fission | Mitosis or meiosis |

### The endomembrane system

The **endomembrane system** is a set of membranes that are linked directly or by **vesicles** (small membrane sacs): the nuclear envelope, rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, vacuoles and the plasma membrane. Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are not part of it.

The pathway of a secreted protein shows how the parts work together:

1. Translation begins on a free ribosome. If the new polypeptide starts with a **signal sequence**, a **signal recognition particle** binds it and docks the ribosome on the **rough ER** (ER studded with ribosomes).
2. The polypeptide is threaded into the ER **lumen** as it is made. There it folds, forms disulfide bonds and has sugar chains added (**glycosylation**).
3. Transport vesicles bud off and fuse with the **cis face** of the **Golgi apparatus**.
4. The Golgi modifies the sugar chains further and sorts proteins. At the **trans face** they are packaged into vesicles bound for the plasma membrane, lysosomes or secretion. Lysosomal enzymes, for example, are tagged with mannose-6-phosphate.
5. **Secretory vesicles** fuse with the plasma membrane and release their contents by **exocytosis**.

The **smooth ER** (no ribosomes) makes lipids such as phospholipids and steroids, detoxifies drugs in liver cells and stores Ca²⁺ (in muscle it is called the sarcoplasmic reticulum). **Lysosomes** contain acid hydrolases that digest worn-out organelles (**autophagy**) and engulfed material. Their internal pH is about 5, so an enzyme that leaks into the cytosol (pH about 7.2) works poorly, which protects the cell.

### Energy organelles and other structures

**Mitochondria** carry out aerobic respiration; their inner membrane is folded into **cristae** that increase the area for the electron transport chain. **Chloroplasts** in plants and algae carry out photosynthesis on stacked **thylakoid** membranes. **Peroxisomes** break down fatty acids and destroy hydrogen peroxide. Plant cells also have a large central **vacuole** that stores water and keeps the cell firm (turgor) and a cellulose **cell wall**.

### The cytoskeleton

The **cytoskeleton** is a network of protein fibres that gives the cell its shape, moves organelles and lets cells move and divide.

| Fibre | Protein subunit | Diameter | Main jobs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Microfilaments | Actin | about 7 nm | Cell shape, muscle contraction (with myosin), cytoplasmic streaming, cleavage furrow |
| Intermediate filaments | Several (e.g. keratins, lamins) | 8–12 nm | Resist tension, anchor the nucleus, form the nuclear lamina |
| Microtubules | α- and β-tubulin dimers | about 25 nm, hollow | Tracks for vesicles, mitotic spindle, cilia and flagella |

Microtubules grow from a **centrosome** in animal cells. **Motor proteins** use ATP to walk along them: **kinesin** usually moves cargo toward the cell edge and **dynein** toward the centre. Eukaryotic cilia and flagella have a **9 + 2** arrangement of microtubules and bend because dynein arms slide neighbouring doublets past each other. This is a completely different mechanism from the rotating bacterial flagellum.

### Endosymbiosis theory

The **endosymbiosis theory** proposes that mitochondria came from an aerobic bacterium (related to modern alphaproteobacteria) that was engulfed by an ancestral host cell and not digested, and that chloroplasts later came from an engulfed **cyanobacterium**. Over time the partners became dependent on each other and many of the bacterial genes moved to the host nucleus. The evidence:

- Both organelles have **two membranes**, as expected if a bacterium was wrapped in host membrane.
- Both contain their own **circular DNA**, not packaged with histones.
- Both have **70S-type ribosomes**, and some antibiotics that block bacterial ribosomes also affect them.
- Both divide by a process like **binary fission** and cannot be made from scratch by the cell.
- They are about the size of bacteria.
- Comparing their rRNA gene sequences places them among bacteria on the tree of life.

### Microscopy basics

**Magnification** is how much bigger the image is than the real object. **Resolution** is the smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as separate. Magnifying past the resolution limit gives a bigger but blurrier image (empty magnification), so resolution is what limits what we can see.

- **Light microscopes** use visible light. Resolution is about 200 nm, limited by the wavelength of light. They can view living cells, and stains or **fluorescent** tags show particular molecules.
- **Transmission electron microscopes (TEM)** pass electrons through very thin sections. Their much shorter wavelength resolves internal structures (ribosomes, membranes) down to a few nanometres in biological samples, but samples must be dead and fixed.
- **Scanning electron microscopes (SEM)** bounce electrons off a coated surface and give 3D-looking images of surfaces.

The key formula:

`magnification = image size ÷ actual size`

Both sizes must be in the **same units**. Remember 1 mm = 1000 µm and 1 µm = 1000 nm.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: actual size from a micrograph

A TEM image shows a mitochondrion 36 mm long. The magnification is ×18 000. How long is the real mitochondrion?

1. Rearrange: actual size = image size ÷ magnification.
2. Convert the image size to µm: 36 mm = 36 000 µm.
3. Actual size = 36 000 µm ÷ 18 000 = **2.0 µm**.

This fits the usual size of a mitochondrion (about 1–10 µm long), which is a useful check.

### Example 2: magnification from a scale bar

A scale bar labelled 10 µm measures 25 mm on a printed micrograph.

1. Convert to the same unit: 25 mm = 25 000 µm.
2. Magnification = 25 000 µm ÷ 10 µm = **×2500**.
3. A nucleus that measures 15 mm on the same image is 15 000 µm ÷ 2500 = 6 µm across.

### Example 3: calibrating an eyepiece graticule

An eyepiece graticule has arbitrary units, so it must be calibrated against a **stage micrometer** for each objective lens. A stage micrometer is 1 mm long, divided into 100 divisions, so each division is 10 µm. Using the ×40 objective, 40 eyepiece units line up with 12 stage divisions.

1. 12 stage divisions = 12 × 10 µm = 120 µm.
2. 1 eyepiece unit = 120 µm ÷ 40 = 3 µm.
3. A cheek cell spans 20 eyepiece units, so it is 20 × 3 µm = **60 µm** across.

If you change to a different objective, the calibration changes and must be repeated.

### Example 4: identifying a cell from data

An unknown cell is 2 µm long, has 70S ribosomes, no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Its wall contains no peptidoglycan. The absence of a nucleus and the 70S ribosomes mean it is a prokaryote. The lack of peptidoglycan points to an **archaeon** rather than a bacterium.

## Common mistakes

- Mixing units in the magnification formula (for example, mm for the image and µm for the cell). Convert first.
- Thinking higher magnification always shows more detail. Resolution, not magnification, sets the limit.
- Saying prokaryotes have no ribosomes. They have 70S ribosomes; they lack membrane-bound organelles.
- Including mitochondria or chloroplasts in the endomembrane system. They are not connected to it by vesicles.
- Describing the 9 + 2 eukaryotic flagellum as rotating like a bacterial flagellum. It bends, driven by dynein.

## Exam tips

- In magnification questions, show the formula, the unit conversion and the final unit. Marks are often given for each step.
- When asked for evidence for endosymbiosis, give specific features (double membrane, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, binary fission) and explain why each supports a bacterial origin.
- For pathway questions, name every organelle in order and say what happens at each stage, not just the list.
- Be ready to identify organelles on TEM images by their membranes and internal structure.

## Key terms

- **Cell theory** — all living things are made of cells, which are the basic unit of life and come from existing cells.
- **Nucleoid** — region of a prokaryotic cell holding its chromosome; not enclosed by a membrane.
- **Plasmid** — small circular DNA molecule separate from the main chromosome.
- **Endomembrane system** — the linked membranes of the nuclear envelope, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles and plasma membrane.
- **Signal sequence** — amino acid sequence at the start of a polypeptide that directs it to the ER.
- **Cytoskeleton** — network of actin microfilaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules.
- **Motor protein** — protein such as kinesin, dynein or myosin that uses ATP to move along a cytoskeletal fibre.
- **Endosymbiosis theory** — idea that mitochondria and chloroplasts came from bacteria engulfed by an ancestral cell.
- **Magnification** — image size divided by actual size.
- **Resolution** — smallest distance at which two points can still be told apart.

## Summary

- Prokaryotes lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, have 70S ribosomes and usually circular DNA; eukaryotes have a nucleus, 80S ribosomes and many organelles.
- The endomembrane system makes, modifies and ships proteins and lipids: rough ER, vesicle, Golgi, vesicle, destination.
- The cytoskeleton (microfilaments, intermediate filaments, microtubules) gives shape, support and movement, using motor proteins.
- Mitochondria and chloroplasts are thought to descend from engulfed bacteria, supported by their membranes, DNA, ribosomes and division.
- Magnification = image size ÷ actual size, using the same units; resolution limits detail.
- Light microscopes resolve about 200 nm and can show living cells; electron microscopes resolve much finer detail in fixed samples.

questions.prompt: Which structure is found in BOTH prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
questions.explanation: All cells need ribosomes to make proteins: prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes and eukaryotes have 80S cytosolic ribosomes. Mitochondria (B) are tempting because prokaryotes respire, but prokaryotes carry out respiration on their plasma membrane and have no membrane-bound organelles.

questions.prompt: Microtubules are polymers of which protein?
questions.explanation: Microtubules are hollow tubes built from α- and β-tubulin dimers. Actin (B) forms the thinner microfilaments, and myosin is a motor protein that moves along actin, not a fibre subunit of microtubules.

questions.prompt: Which observation provides the strongest evidence that mitochondria descended from free-living bacteria?

options.A: Mitochondria produce most of the cell's ATP
options.B: Mitochondria are found in nearly all eukaryotic cells
options.C: Mitochondria are surrounded by cytosol containing 80S ribosomes
options.D: Mitochondria contain circular DNA and 70S-type ribosomes, and divide by a fission-like process

questions.explanation: Circular DNA, bacterial-type ribosomes and fission are features shared with bacteria, so they point to a bacterial ancestor. Producing ATP (A) is the mitochondrion's job, but many cells and organisms make ATP, so it says nothing about where mitochondria came from.

questions.prompt: A pancreatic cell makes and secretes a digestive enzyme. Which sequence correctly describes the path of the enzyme?

options.A: Free ribosome → Golgi apparatus → rough ER → lysosome → plasma membrane
options.B: Rough ER → transport vesicle → Golgi apparatus → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane
options.C: Smooth ER → rough ER → secretory vesicle → Golgi apparatus → plasma membrane
options.D: Nucleus → rough ER → mitochondrion → Golgi apparatus → plasma membrane

questions.explanation: Secreted proteins are made on ribosomes attached to the rough ER, carried in vesicles to the Golgi for modification and sorting, then packaged in secretory vesicles that fuse with the plasma membrane. Option A puts the Golgi before the ER and sends the protein to a lysosome, which is the destination for lysosomal enzymes, not secreted ones.

questions.prompt: A student increases the magnification of a light microscope from ×400 to ×2000 but still cannot see ribosomes. What is the best explanation?

options.A: Ribosomes are only present in living cells, and the slide was fixed
options.B: The magnification is still not high enough; ×10 000 would show them
options.C: Ribosomes are transparent and cannot be stained
options.D: Ribosomes (about 25 nm) are smaller than the resolution limit of light microscopy (about 200 nm)

questions.explanation: Resolution, set by the wavelength of visible light, limits a light microscope to about 200 nm. Ribosomes are far smaller, so extra magnification only enlarges a blur. Option B is the common misconception that magnification alone reveals detail.

questions.prompt: On a TEM image at ×12 000 magnification, a mitochondrion measures 24 mm long. What is its actual length?
questions.explanation: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification = 24 000 µm ÷ 12 000 = 2 µm. Option B results from a unit-conversion slip (using 2400 µm), and D comes from multiplying instead of dividing.

questions.prompt: A scale bar labelled 5 µm measures 20 mm on a micrograph. What is the magnification of the image?
questions.explanation: Convert 20 mm to 20 000 µm, then magnification = 20 000 µm ÷ 5 µm = ×4000. Option A comes from dividing 20 by 5 without converting units.

questions.prompt: A newly discovered single-celled organism has 70S ribosomes, no nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles and a cell wall with no peptidoglycan. It is most likely a:
questions.explanation: No nucleus and 70S ribosomes mean a prokaryote, and the lack of peptidoglycan in the wall separates archaea from bacteria. A cyanobacterium (A) is a prokaryote too, but as a bacterium it has peptidoglycan in its wall.
